messages.subject: Re: Program Distance Question (fwd)
parts:
Hi Scott,

I'm cc'ing my reply to the distance-sampling list as this is a question that
comes up fairly often:

On Wed, 10 Dec 2003 09:33:50 -0600, Scott Somershoe wrote:


> >Len,
> > Thanks again for your help. I think things are rolling smoothly now.
> >One question, I get a warning saying "Parameters are being constrained to
> >obtain monotonicity." Is this a problem I need to worry about?

The short answer is usually not.

Here's the long answer. Under most circumstances we expect a priori that true
detection function is a monotonicly non-increasing function of distance from the
point or line (i.e., the further the object is from the point or line, the lower
the probabilty of detection). Therefore, by default, Distance tries to ensure
that the fitted function is monotonic non-increasing. It does this by
evaluating the detection function g(x) at a set of evenly spaced distances (x's)
from 0 (x0) to the truncation distance (x9), and it makes sure that g(x0)>=g
(x1)>=g(x2)>=... >= g(x9). There are other options in Model Definition |
Detection function | Constraints, and these are documented in the online manual.

Under most circumstances, the fitted function does not come up against this
constraint -- in other words the data indicate that the function should be
monotonic non-increasing. However, under some circumstances the data call for a
non-monotonic function, so the constraint is triggered and that is why you get
the warning message. The estimates you end up with are no longer maximum
likelihood estimates, but are constrained maximum likelihood estimates.

The commonest case where this happens is where you have a relatively small
dataset and just by chance there is a small "bump" at some distance, which
Distance would try to fit with an extra adjustment term, were it not for the
monotonicity constraint. Such models are usually over-parameterized (too many
adjustment terms) and are not chosen using model selection criteria such as AIC.
You can see this in the D4Ducknest example project -- the half-normal+cosine
model gives a monotonicity warning when the first cosine term is added, but then
that model has an AIC of 1.5 worse than the plain half-normal model, so is not
selected. See the Model Fitting page of results for that analysis. (If you
want to see the effect of the constraint, try running an analysis with half-
normal + 1 cosine adjustment manually selected and no constraints.)

You can also get this occuring where there is a problem in your dataset such as
evasive movement of animals, which leads to "too few" animals close to the line
or point, and "too many" away from it. In this case, you don't want to fit the
data, but instead you want your fitted detection function to be "too high" close
to the line or point and "too low" away from it. Fitting a hazard rate or half-
normal key function with few or no adjustments and monotonicity constraint
turned on will achieve this. (An alternative with such data is to put the data
into intervals, as I think has been discussed in previous postings.)

If a function that has been constrained is the one selected by Distance then
there is a minor problem with the estimate of the variance of f(0). This is
because the fit is no longer the maximum likelihood fit (because of the
constraint) so the theory used in deriving the variance isn't valid. However,
in practice this isn't something to worry about. In any case, we recommend
deriving final variance estimates for D or N using a nonparametric bootstrap,
resampling by transects, so the analytic variance of f(0) becomes irrelevant.

So, in summary, if you see this message, you should look at the Model Fitting
page of results to see which function it was fitting when the message occured.
Was that function selected? If not, it's likely just a symptom that the model
not selected had too many parameters. Also look again at your data and ask
yourself why was the constraint hit -- is there some problem in your data (such
as evasive movement), or was it likely due to one histogram bar being slightly
higher than previous bars just due to chance (as with the Ducknest data). The
histogram plots and Chi-sq goodness of fit tests will be useful in answering
this.

Hope this helps,

- Len
